scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Legend traces Geommu to the Three Kingdoms period around 660 AD in Silla.

Chronicled in sources like Samguk yusa and Donggyeong japgi, tales tell of Hwangchang (a boy sword dancer who killed the king of Baekje and was executed) and Gwanchang (a young Hwarang warrior slain in battle).
Memorial dances wearing masks imitating Hwangchang were known as Hwangchangmu.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally a memorial and court entertainment performance, Geommu bridges military symbolism and theatrical elegance.
In Jinju, the dance is prominently performed during an annual memorial ritual honoring Nongae, a patriot kisaeng who died taking a Japanese general off a cliff during wartime.
Modern performances take place at cultural heritage centers, national theaters, and traditional arts festivals.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Geommu is performed by a group of 6 to 8 female dancers working through chum-sawi (dance movements) and changdan (rhythmic cycles).

Performance centers on three primary movement patterns: Ipchum-sawi (dancers standing in two facing rows), Anjeon-sawi (dancers executing floorwork while kneeling in the two-row formation), and Yeonpungdae (dancers forming a circular pattern and spinning in rotation).
Watch for Ipchum-sawi, Anjeon-sawi, Yeonpungdae.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (d11H2pJc7lQ)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Transitions between two facing parallel lines (Ipchum-sawi, Anjeon-sawi) and a revolving group circle (Yeonpungdae).

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Geommu is accompanied by Samhyeon-nyukgak, a traditional six-instrument ensemble comprising two piri (bamboo double-reed oboes), one daegeum (large bamboo transverse flute), one haegeum (two-string bowed fiddle), one janggu (double-headed hourglass drum), and one buk (barrel drum).
The janggu uses different leather skins on each head to produce distinct pitches, while the buk is struck with an open hand and a wooden stick.
Listen for the Piri (2), Daegeum, Haegeum, Janggu.
The pulse is Varied changdan meters at about 100 beats a minute.

A wind-and-percussion soundscape dominated by the resonant bamboo reeding of twin piri and the breathy transverse tones of the daegeum, underpinned by the dual-pitched skin tones of the janggu drum, punctuated by the metallic clinking of sword rings.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performers wear a stylized Joseon Dynasty military uniform over a hanbok.
The costume consists of a chima (skirt), jeogori (jacket), kwaeja or jeonbok (military overcoat), and jeon-dae or hongtti (wide red chest sash).

Dancers wear a black military-style cap (jeon-rip or jeollip) tied under the chin with dangling red and yellow beads and a red tassel, along with thick white socks (beoseon) and detachable striped sleeve covers (saektonghansam).

scenes.title: The people
narration: Historical accounts credit Horace Newton Allen with writing the first detailed Western eyewitness description of the dance in 1896.
In the 1950s, traditional cultural promoter Park Heonbong led the reconstruction of Jinju Geommu by interviewing and working with eight surviving female dancers.
Jinju Geommu is the primary court-derived variant, originating in Jinju and characterized by blue skirts and jade green jackets.
Traces from ancient Silla sword rituals and Hwangchangmu mask dances to Joseon court Kisaeng repertoire taught at Gwonbeon institutions, preserved today as Intangible Cultural Property No. 12.

scenes.title: Body and posture
narration: Upright, graceful court posture with broad shoulder carriage to accommodate military overcoats and headpiece balance.
Fluid arm swoops using extended striped sleeve covers (saektonghansam), shifting to rapid hilt twirling of twin short blades.
Controlled torso stability during kneeling drops; slight fluid rotation of upper body during sword flourishes.

wardrobe.from_sources: Performers wear a stylized Joseon Dynasty military uniform over a hanbok. The costume consists of a chima (skirt), jeogori (jacket), kwaeja or jeonbok (military overcoat), and jeon-dae or hongtti (wide red chest sash). Dancers wear a black military-style cap (jeon-rip or jeollip) tied under the chin with dangling red and yellow beads and a red tassel, along with thick white socks (beoseon) and detachable striped sleeve covers (saektonghansam). Regional variants dictate skirt and jacket colors, such as Jinju's blue skirt and jade green jacket. Dancers carry paired short swords (dangeom/kal) made of nickel-brass alloy (baektong) measuring 22 cm, featuring three attached rings between hilt and blade that sound during movement.
